title: Be More Spock: Spacing, Interleaving and Desirable Difficulties
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles draws on the Bjork lab's work to argue that curriculum timings must be reorganised if students are to remember what is taught. For spacing, interleaving and desirable difficulties he sets out a quoted finding followed by a practical implication. His proposals: assess previously taught content rather than only the latest topic, map retrievals across years 7 to 11, split units into interleaved chunks, and disrupt lessons with unrelated retrieval. He reports that classes split between teachers progressed faster, and concludes that the alternative is to blame pupils for forgetting.
points: End-of-topic tests of recent content tell little about long-term retention; assessments should mainly test earlier material.
Plan an assessment map across years with deliberately widening gaps between retrievals.
Interleaving new content creates spaced learning, so cycling short blocks across units beats long single-topic units.
Lessons that feel coherent and easy can produce weaker long-term learning than disjointed, harder practice.
If curriculum timing ignores cognitive science, forgetting gets blamed on pupils.
quotes: Instead, at the end of the topic we should test previously taught topics in our assessments (and perhaps mainly test those). This will tell us what students are retaining in long-term memory, and help build that long-term memory.
This means that we have to plan an assessment map from year 7 through to year 11, working out the optimum gaps between retrievals and assessments.
However, if you practise interleaving of new content, you effectively create spaced learning. This has profound implications.
I have tested this repeatedly when the timetable has split classes between two and three teachers. I always asked those teachers to teach different parts of the curriculum.
we assume that we need to study the same content in a lesson for it to be coherent. This is incorrect – it feels coherent – but this makes it easier to forget.

Although this would feel disjointed and confusing, it would lead to greater long-term memory, not least because students would make unexpected connections between characters, developing a more profound schema than if they had studied them separately.
Cognitive science tells you that you must reorganise the timings of your curriculum if you want students to remember what you have taught.
